--- title: "CO2_web" format: html editor: visual --- # Applying ideal gas law All the calculations begin with the ideal gas law: $$p \times V = n \times R \times T \hspace{75mm}(eq. 1),$$ where $p$ is pressure, $V$ is volume, $n$ is number of moles of ideal gas, $R$ is universal gas constant, and $T$ is temperature. The first key consideration is ensuring unit comparability. If we arbitrarily select $R = 8.314 \frac{J}{mol \times K}$, $T$ must be in Kelvins (K), $n$ in moles, $p$ in Pascals (Pa), and $V$ in cubic meters ($m^{3}$) since the derived units joules and pascals are defined as $J = \frac{kg \times m^{2}}{s^{2}}$ and $Pa = \frac{kg}{m \times s^{2}}$, respectively: $$\frac{kg}{m \times s^{2}}(p) \times m^{3}(V) = mol(n) \times \frac{kg \times m^{2}}{s^{2} \times mol \times K}(R) \times K(T) \Longrightarrow \frac{kg \times m^2}{s^2} = \frac{kg \times m^2}{s^2} \hspace{10mm}(eq. 2).$$ It may be convenient to redefine the units to express volume of container headspace in mL instead of cubic meters and express the gas pressure in atmospheres instead of Pascals. At the see level, atmospheric pressure is 1 atmosphere (atm), which is a very convenient number. If we choose to use atm as the unit of pressure, the value of universal gas constant $R$ must be expressed as $R = 0.082 \frac{L \times atm}{mol \times K}$. Furthermore, by expressing $V$ in the more convenient unit of mL while keeping K as the unit of temperature, $n$ will be expressed in mmol. Since we are interested in concentration of $CO_{2}$ in the headspace of closed container, eq. 1 is solved in respect to $n$: $$n = \frac{p \times V}{R \times T} \hspace{75mm}(eq. 3).$$ Equation 3 applies to all gases in the entire headspace of the container. However, we are only interested in $CO_{2}$, which occupies a fraction of the headspace. Gas chromatography typically returns the concentration of headspace $CO_{2}$ in ppm (parts per million). It is convenient to define a new variable $\beta$ representing the measured $CO_{2}$ concentration in ppm. For example, if $\beta$ is e.g. 450 ppm at the beginning of an incubation, then the partial pressure of $CO_{2}$ (usually denoted as $pCO_{2}$) in the headspace of a container that has been closed at atmospheric pressure 1 atm is then $\beta \times 10^{-6} \times p = 450 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 = 0.000450~atm~(pCO_{2})$. The partial pressure of $CO_{2}$ in atm is function of $CO_{2}$ concentration in ppm and pressure in atm. Since gas chromatography usually returns $CO_{2}$ concentration in ppm, we will use variable $\beta$ in all equations below rather than $pCO_{2}$. If the container's headspace volume is e.g. 100 mL and the container is held at a temperature of $20°C = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K$, the headspace $CO_{2}$ concentration is: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

It is important to note that all other variables stay the same. Although the procedure may seem straightforward, **several aspects require careful attention**. In following sections, we will gradually discuss quantitatively the most important aspects - headspace pressure change and $CO_2$ dissolution as affected by temperature, volume of soil solution, its acidity/alkalinity and ionic strength. ### Change of headspace pressure Laboratory incubations are almost always performed at constant temperature so the variable $T$ in all equations above is well defined. However, a potential issue arises if the incubation temperature differs from the temperature at which the container was sealed (typically room temperature), as this leads to a change in headspace pressure due to thermal expansion or contraction of the gas. The effect of temperature change on pressure change can be calculated using eq. 1. $V$ of the container does not change and, for simplicity, $n$ can be considered constant for some brief period of time. Any change of $T$ must be compensated by the change of $p$: $$\frac{p_1}{T_1} = \frac{p_2}{T_2} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 6).$$ The change of $p$ from $p_1$, previously defined as 1 atm, to $p_2$ can be expressed as a function of $T_1$ and $T_2$: $$\Delta p = p_2 - p_1 = p_1 \times (\frac{T_2}{T_1} - 1) \hspace{75mm} (eq. 7).$$ If the container is closed at a room temperature of $20°C = T_1 = 293.15K$ and then stored in an incubator set to $30°C = T_2 = 303.15K$, the headspace pressure change is: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

To correct for the change in temperature, the overpressure, defined by the term $(\frac{T_2}{T_1} - 1)$ can be released so that $p_2 = p_1$, or the result of Eq. 5 is calculated only with values of $p_1$ (1 atm) and $T_2$ (303.15 K). $$\Delta CO_{2}(\Delta p=0) = \frac{\beta \times 10^{-6} \times p_1 \times V}{R \times T_2} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 9).$$ If $T_2$ differs from $T_1$ and the pressure changed, we need to use $p_2$, which is a function of $p_1$, $T_1$ and $T_2$ ($p_2 = p_1 \times \frac{T_2}{T_1}$): $$\Delta CO_{2}(\Delta p \neq 0) = \frac{\beta \times 10^{-6} \times p_1 \times \frac{T_2}{T_1} \times V}{R \times T_2} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 10).$$ The relative error associated with disregarding the pressure change induced by a change in $T$ can be defined with respect to $\Delta CO_{2}(\Delta p \neq 0)$ for example using the following equation that combines eqs. 5 and 10: $$Error (\%) = (\frac{\Delta CO_{2}(\Delta p=0)}{\Delta CO_{2}(\Delta p \neq 0)}-1) \times 100 = (\frac{T_1}{T_2}-1) \times 100 \hspace{75mm} (eq. 11).$$ If $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{293.15}{303.15}$, the relative error in the calculated $CO_2$ concentration due to the invalid assumption that the headspace pressure remains constant is: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: $~$ $$Error (\%) = (\frac{293.15}{303.15}-1) \times 100 = -3.3 \% \hspace{75mm} (eq. 12).$$ $~$ Our result is underestimated by approx. 3%. If the $T_2$ is lower than $T_1$, e.g. the temperature in incubation vessel is lowered to $5°C = 278.15K$, the relative error is $(\frac{293.15}{273.15}-1) \times 100 = 5.4 \%$ thus, the result is slightly overestimated. An underestimation of the result by 10% is achieved when incubation temperature $T_2$ is around 50°C.\ The pressure in the headspace can be also affected by unbalanced exchange of gasses between the soil and headspace. In aerobic incubations, $CO_2$ production is frequently assumed to be perfectly balanced by $O_2$ consumption, i.e. there is one mole of consumed $O_2$ per one mole of produced $CO_2$. However, this 1:1 ratio, so called respiration quotient, is not always reached even under aerobic conditions. It could be as high as 1.75 or close to 0.1 (Dilly, 2001, 2003 and 2004, Capek et al., 2015). Ratio higher than 1 causes increase of pressure and vice versa. Great change in headspace pressure could be expected in anaerobic incubations as the increase in $CO_2$ concentration is not compensated for by the $O_2$ consumption. The effects of respiration quotient other than 1 and anaerobiosis on headspace pressure change is beyond the scope of this document so it will not be discussed further. #### Example: Temperature sensitivity of respiration (case 1) The sensitivity of soil respiration to temperature was commonly expressed as a $Q_{10}$, i.e. a parameter which defines the relative change in respiration (i.e. change in $pCO_2$ in the vessel) with a temperature change of 10°C: $$Q_{10} = \frac{\Delta CO_2(T_2)}{\Delta CO_2(T_1)}^{\frac{10}{T_2 - T_1}} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 13).$$ We will arbitrarily select $Q_{10}$ 2, i.e. $\Delta CO_2(T_2)$ is 2 times greater than $\Delta CO_2(T_1)$ when $T_2 - T_1 = 10°C$. Even though the $Q_{10}$ concept is nowadays considered inaccurate, its relative simplicity will allow us to easily quantify the error caused by headspace pressure change. If $T_2 - T_1 = 10°C$, $Q_{10}$ can simply be calculated using respiration measured at two different temperatures. We can simply assume that $T_1$ is laboratory temperature 20°C and $T_2$ is then 30°C. Using two measured respiration rates, calculated $Q_{10}$ was experimentally estimated to be 2. However, the headspace pressure change was ignored when respiration at 30°C was calculated. If the respiration is recalculated applying eq. 6, $Q_{10}$ changes from 2 to: $$Q_{10} = 2 \times \frac{T_2}{T_1} = 2 \times \frac{393.15}{293.15} = 2.07 \hspace{75mm} (eq. 14).$$ This change represents the relative error of 3.5%. # Dissolution of $CO_2$ in acidic soils The headspace $CO_2$ represents only a fraction of the total inorganic carbon (IC) in a closed incubation container with a soil sample. This is because $CO_2$ is soluble and can dissolve in soil water. If the dissolved $CO_2$ is ignored, the respiration rate calculated from $\Delta \beta$ (eq. 5) may be underestimated. The dissolution process is governed by the following equilibrium reaction: $$CO_2(gas) \rightleftarrows CO_2(aq)^{*} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 15).$$ According to Henry's law, the $CO_2$ dissolved in (soil) water as $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ (here $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ represents the sum of $CO_2(aq)$ and $H_2CO_3$) is proportional to the partial pressure of $CO_2$ in the container's headspace, which is $\Delta \beta \times 10^{-6} \times p$ in eq. 4. We assume that there is an equilibrium between the two forms of IC (see below). At that equilibrium, $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ can be calculated from measured $\beta$ using an equation: $$CO_2(aq)^{*} = K_H \times \beta \times 10^{-6} \times p \hspace{75mm} (eq. 16),$$ in which $K_H$ is Henry's law constant in $\frac{mol}{L \times atm}$ of the reaction described by eq. 15. Eq. 16 was simplified to allow a straightforward calculation. Eq. 16 is frequently transformed by a decadic logarithm and $K_H$ is expressed as $pK_H$: $$log(CO_2(aq)^{*}) = pK_H + log(\beta \times 10^{-6}) + log(p) \hspace{75mm} (eq. 17).$$ $pK_H$ is an experimentally derived constant, which is temperature dependent. According to Plummer and Busenberg (1982), the relationship between $pK_H$ and T (in K again) is: $$pK_H = 108.3865 + 0.01985076 \times T - 6919.53 \times \frac{1}{T} - 40.45154 \times log(T) + 669356 \times \frac{1}{T^2} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 18).$$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![***Figure 1***: *Relationship between the temperature and Henry's law constant $pK_H$ for $CO_2$.*](respiration_files/figure-html/Rscript (5) plotting pK0 against T according to eq. 18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: As shown in figure 1, $pK_H$ decreases (within values -1.109 and -1.711) with increasing temperature between 0 and 50°C (i.e. 273.15 and 323.15K). This means that the solubility of $CO_2$ in water decreases with increasing temperature. Knowing the experimentally derived value of $pK_H$, the concentration of $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ in soil solution (in moles of $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ per liter) can be calculated. However, our interest lies not in concentration, but in the absolute amount of $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ within the closed container. This allows direct comparison to the amount of $CO_2$ in the headspace calculated by eqs. 4 and 5. To obtain the absolute amount of $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ in moles, the $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ concentration in $mol \times L^{-1}$ is multiplied by the volume of soil water in mL ($V_s$). The result is then in mmols (i.e. 1 mole of $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ contains 1 mole of IC. Let's assume that we incubate 10 grams of fresh organic soil with a pH around 4. This can be defined quantitatively. - **Soil water content** At a constant temperature, e.g. 20°C, the relative proportion between $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ and $CO_2$ in % can be easily expressed when eqs. 4 (ideal gas law) and 16 are combined: $$\frac{CO_2(aq)^{*}}{CO_2} \times 100 = 10^{pK_H} \times \beta \times 10^{-6} \times p \times V_s \times \frac{R \times T}{ \beta \times 10^{-6} \times p \times V} \times 100= 10^{pK_H} \times R \times T \times \frac{V_s}{V} \times 100 \hspace{10mm} (eq. 21).$$ Because $10^{pK_H}$, $R$ and $T$ are constant and the product of their multiplication at 20°C is always 0.94, the relative proportion between $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ and $CO_2$ is entirely defined by the ratio of soil water volume to headspace volume, both being in mL. If the \$ \frac{V_s}{V} = \frac{8}{100} = 0.08\$ as in eqs. 5 and 19, the result of eq. 21 is $0.94 \times \frac{8}{100} \times 100 = 7.5 \%$. When we plot the effect of temperature as we did for the effect of water content in figure 2, the slope of the linear relationship decreases with increasing temperature. This means that **the amount of IC in the water phase of the sample increases with decreasing temperatures**. The following graph shows the relationship between $\frac{V_s}{V}$ and $\frac{CO_2(aq)^{*}}{CO_2}$ at the three different temperatures - 0, 20 and 30°C: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![***Figure 3***: *Relationship between the relative amount of $CO_2(aq)^{*}$ $CO_2(gas)$ and relative volume of soil water $V_s$ in respect to headspace volume $V$ in a closed cotainer incubated at three different temperatures 0, 20 and 30°C*](respiration_files/figure-html/Rscript (8) Applying eq 21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Ignoring $CO_2$ dissolution has little effect on the calculated respiration rates in acidic soils with low moisture, large headspace, and high temperature. However, respiration is likely underestimated due to high $CO_2$ solubility in wet soils or peat samples incubated in small containers at low temperatures. #### Example: Temperature sensitivity of respiration (case 2) In the following we will extend the effect of headspace pressure change on temperature sensitivity in case 1 for the effect of $CO_2$ dissolution in acidic soil water, including the temperature sensitive $pK_H$. To do so, we combine eq. 13 with the ideal gas law (eq. 3), for two different temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ (whose difference is 10°C again). We can to express the apparent $Q_{10}^{app}$ as a function of $\Delta \beta_1$ and $\Delta \beta_2$ measured at the GC for $T_1$ and $T_2$: $$Q_{10}^{app} = \frac{\Delta CO_2(T_2)}{\Delta CO_2(T_1)} = \frac{\frac{\Delta \beta_2 \times 10^{-6} \times p \times V}{R \times T_2}}{\frac{\Delta \beta_1 \times 10^{-6} \times p \times V}{R \times T_1}} = \frac{\Delta \beta_2}{\Delta \beta_1} \times \frac{T_1}{T_2} = 2 \hspace{10mm} (eq. 22).$$ We assume that $Q_{10}^{app}$ is 2. Now, we will calculate the true $Q_{10}$ that considers all forms of IC in our closed incubation container, i.e. $CO_2$ and $CO_2(aq)^{*}$. To do so, $Q_{10}$ is calculated using following equation: $$Q_{10} = \frac{\Delta CO_2(T_2) + \Delta CO_2(aq)^{*}(T_2)}{\Delta CO_2(T_1) + \Delta CO_2(aq)^{*}(T_1)} = \frac{\Delta \beta_2}{\Delta \beta_1} \times \frac{\frac{V}{R \times T_2} + 10^{pK_H(T_2) \times V_s}}{\frac{V}{R \times T_1} + 10^{pK_H(T_1) \times V_s}} \hspace{10mm} (eq. 23).$$ By combining eqs. 22 and 23, we obtain the following equation: $$Q_{10} = Q_{10}^{app} \times \frac{T_2}{T_1} \times \frac{\frac{V}{R \times T_2} + 10^{pK_H(T_2) \times V_s}}{\frac{V}{R \times T_1} + 10^{pK_H(T_1) \times V_s}} \hspace{10mm} (eq. 24).$$ $Q_{10}$ is first calculated for a scenario with $V = 100mL$, $V_s = 8 mL$, $T_1$ and $T_2$ are 20 and 30°C, respectively: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The respective equilibria are defined as: $$K_1 = \frac{H^+ \times HCO_3^-}{CO_2(aq)^{*}} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 28),$$ $$K_2 = \frac{H^+ \times CO_3^{-2}}{HCO_3^-} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 29).$$ Both equations can be again transformed by decadic logarithm. The presence of various charged chemical species in soil solution directly affects Henry's law constant $pK_H$ and activity of $H^+$, $HCO_3^{-}$ and $CO_3^{-2}$. It is thus necessary to extend the theory further to acknowledge the effect of soil solution chemistry. In next two sections, we will first discuss the activity of $H^+$, $HCO_3^{-}$ and $CO_3^{-2}$ by applying Debye–Hückel equation because the respective mathematical expression is not that difficult to grasp. Then, we will explain the effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ by applying Sechenov relationship in its extended form as presented by Weisenberger and Schumpe (1996). ## Estimating activity coefficients using the Debye–Hückel equation There is a difference between the concentration and the activity of charged species including $HCO_3^-$, $CO_3^{-2}$ and $H^+$. While the concentration refers to the amount of substance per unit volume (e.g. $mol \times L^{-1}$), the activity reflects the effective concentration, accounting for interactions between ions in solution. These interactions are significant for all charged species, including $H^+$, $HCO_3^-$, $CO_3^{-2}$, and other cations and anions. The relationship between activity and concentration is defined by an equation: $$a_s = \gamma_s \times [S] \hspace{75mm} (eq. 47),$$ in which $a_s$ is an activity of charged species of interest, $[S]$ is its concentration in $mol \times L^{-1}$, and $\gamma_s$ is nondimensional activity coefficient. The constants $pK_1$ and $pK_2$ have been defined for activities of charged species, not concentrations. It is therefore important to determine what could be the error of our calculations when we ignore activity coefficients. To do so, we need to calculate activity coefficients first. This can be achieved by using Debye-Huckel equation: $$log(\gamma_i) = - \frac{A \times z_i^2 \times \sqrt I}{1 + B \times \alpha_i \times \sqrt I} \hspace{75mm} (eq. 48),$$ in which $z_i$ is charge of ion $i$, $\alpha_i$ is its effective size in Angstroms (i.e. 1A = 0.1 nm), $I$ is the ionic strength of soil solution in $mol \times L^{-1}$, $A$ and $B$ are coefficients of the equation with dimensions $\frac{L^{0.5}}{mol^{0.5}}$ and $\frac{L^{0.5}}{A \times mol^{0.5}}$, respectively. There are five different variables in eq. 48, which needs to be known to calculate $\gamma_{i}$. One that can be directly calculated is $I$ because: $$I = \frac{1}{2} \times \sum c_i \times z_i^2 \hspace{75mm} (eq. 49).$$ In eq. 49, $c_i$ is the concentration of ion $i$ in $mol \times L^{-1}$ and $z_i$ is its charge. There is one more confounding effect of soil solution chemistry, which will be discussed in following section. ## Estimating effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ using Sechenov relationship The concentration of ions in soil solution affects not only the activity coefficients but also the solubility of $CO_2$ through Henry's law constant $pK_H$. Unfortunately, the mathematical expression of this effect is difficult to apply accurately in case of soil solution, because several different ions are typically present in there. The general relationship between $pK_H$ and concentration of ions in soil solution is defined by following equation: $$pK_H = pK_{H,0} - \sum[h_i + h_{G,0} + h_T \times (T-298.15)] \times c_i \hspace{75mm} (eq. 63).$$ in which $pK_{H,0}$ is Henry's law constant for pure water (eq. 18), $pK_H$ is the constant for a solution that contains several ions ($i$). Concentration of each ion in $mol \times L^{-1}$ is defined by variable $c_i$ and its effect on $pK_H$ is defined by a empirically estimated parameter $h_i$ in $L \times mol^{-1}$. Finally, variables $h_{G,0}$ (in $L \times mol^{-1}$) and $h_T$ (in $L \times mol^{-1} \times K^{-1}$) are two gas specific (i.e. $CO_2$ specific in this case) variables, again experimentally derived. The first applies to standard temperature 298.15 °C, and the second defines the temperature sensitivity. Every gas has its own $h_{G,0}$ and $h_T$, and every ion present in soil solution has its own $h_i$. Eq. 63 cannot be applied if concentrations of all ions in soil solution are not known. This is the reason for why the eq. 63 is so difficult to use. Concentrations of all ions in soil solution is rarely known and that limits the use of eq. 63. We will use the data of Stednick (1984) reported above to quantify the effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$. According to Weisenberger and Schumpe (1996), $CO_2$ specific variables $h_{G,0}$ and $h_T$ are respectively $-0.0172~L \times mol^{-1}$ and $-0.338 \times 10^{-3}~L \times mol^{-1}$. At 20°C (293.15 K), $-0.0172 - 0.338 \times 10^{-3} \times (293.15 - 298.15) = -0.01551$ is added to all $h_i$ of all ions in soil solution. Values of $h_i$ of each ion measured by Stednick (1984) in soil solution are reported in the table below. | Ion | $h_i$ in $L \times mol^{-1}$ | Concentrations in $\mu mol \times L^{-1}$ | |:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:----------------------:| | $H^+$ | 0 | 1.6 | | $K^+$ | 0.0922 | 15 | | $Ca^{+2}$ | 0.1762 | 40 | | $Mg^{+2}$ | 0.1694 | 23.5 | | $Na^+$ | 0.1143 | 96 | | $Fe^{+2}$ | 0.1523 | 0.3 | | $SO_4^{-2}$ | 0.1172 | 130 | | $Cl^-$ | 0.0318 | 273 | According to eq. 18, $pK_{H,0}$ is -1.41 at 20°C. Applying the eq. 63, $pK_H$ is expected to be: $$pK_H = -1.41 - [(0 -0.01551) \times 1.6 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (H^+)\\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.0922 -0.01551) \times 15 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (K^+) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1762 -0.01551) \times 40 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Ca^{+2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1694 -0.01551) \times 23.5 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Mg^{+2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1143 -0.01551) \times 96 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Na^{+}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1523 -0.01551) \times 0.3 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Fe^{+2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1172 -0.01551) \times 130 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (SO_4^{-2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.0318 -0.01551) \times 273 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Cl^{-}) \\ \hspace{20mm} = -1.41 - 5.52 \times 10^{-5} \approx -1.41 \hspace{20mm} (eq. 64)$$ The effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ is negligible in this case. Eq. 63 is typically used to calculate $CO_2$ solubility in see water with nearly molar concentrations of $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$. Thus, the effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ could be neglected in most of soils. This effect, however, becomes significant in very saline soils or in soils. Let's document it on an example. In the following example, we will use eq. 63 to calculate $pK_H$ of $CO_2$ for dry steppe solonetz using measured ion concentrations reported in Endovitsky et al. (2014). The ion concentrations are reported in a table below: | Ion | $h_i$ in $L \times mol^{-1}$ | Concentrations in $mmol \times L^{-1}$ | |:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:----------------------:| | $HCO_3^-$ | 0.0967 | 8.88 | | $CO_3^{-2}$ | 0.1423 | 0.72 | | $Ca^{+2}$ | 0.1762 | 9.73 | | $Mg^{+2}$ | 0.1694 | 77.5 | | $Na^+$ | 0.1143 | 270.4 | | $SO_4^{-2}$ | 0.1172 | 137.2 | | $Cl^-$ | 0.0318 | 160.2 | According to reported soil solution composition, $pK_H$ at 20°C is expected to be: $$pK_H = -1.41 - [(0.0967 -0.01551) \times 8.88 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (HCO_3^-)\\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1423 -0.01551) \times 0.72 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (CO_3^{-2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1762 -0.01551) \times 9.73 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Ca^{+2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1694 -0.01551) \times 77.5 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Mg^{+2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1143 -0.01551) \times 270.4 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Na^{+}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.1172 -0.01551) \times 137.2 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (SO_4^{-2}) \\ \hspace{20mm} + (0.0318 -0.01551) \times 160.2 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Cl^{-}) \\ \hspace{20mm} = -1.41 - 0.0576 = -1.468 \hspace{20mm} (eq. 65)$$ As compared to $pK_{H,0}$, $pK_H$ is lower so the $CO_2$ solubility decreases in this saline soil by $(1 - 10^{-1.468 + 1.41}) \times 100 = 12.5 \%$. Nevertheless, the salinity also affects the dissociation due to high ionic strength of the solution. Let's compare decrease in solubility with the effect of high ionic strength on the dissociation. To perform the comparison, we need to calculate ionic strength of soil solution using eq. 49: $$I = \frac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{2} \times (8.88 \times 1^2 [HCO_3^{-}] + 0.72 \times 2^2 [CO_3^{-2}] + 9.73 \times 2^2 [Ca^{+2}]+ 77.5 \times 2^2[Mg^{+2}] + 270.4 \times 1^2 [Na^+] + 137.4 \times 2^2 [SO_4^{-2}] + 16.2 \times 1^2 [Cl^-]) = 0.6~mol \times L \hspace{75mm} (eq. 66).$$ Knowing the ionic strength, we can further calculate activity coefficients $\gamma_{HCO_3^-}$, $\gamma_{CO_3^{-2}}$ and $\gamma_{H^+}$ using eqs. 51 - 53: $$\gamma_{HCO_3^-} = 10^{- \frac{0.507 \times 1^2 \times \sqrt 0.6}{1 + 0.3282 \times 5.4 \times \sqrt 0.6}} = 0.68 \hspace{75mm} (eq. 67),$$ $$\gamma_{CO_3^{-2}} = 10^{- \frac{0.507 \times 2^2 \times \sqrt 0.6}{1 + 0.3282 \times 5.4 \times \sqrt0.6}} = 0.22 \hspace{75mm} (eq. 68),$$ $$\gamma_{H^{+}} = 10^{- \frac{0.507 \times 1^2 \times \sqrt 0.6}{1 + 0.3282 \times 9 \times \sqrt 0.6}} = 0.76 \hspace{75mm} (eq. 69),$$ Finally, we can quantify the relative change in the amount of IC in soil solution with a composition reported above and pH of 8.85 as compared to pure water using an equation: $$\Delta IC [\%] =(\frac{10^{pK_H} + 10^{pK_H + pK_1 + pH - log(\gamma_{H^+}) - log(\gamma_{HCO_3^-})} + 10^{pK_H + pK_1 + pK_2 + 2\times pH - 2 \times log(\gamma_{H^+}) - log(\gamma_{CO_3^{-2}})}}{10^{pK_{H, 0}} + 10^{pK_{H, 0} + pK_1 + pH} + 10^{pK_{H, 0} + pK_1 + pK_2 + 2\times pH}} - 1) \times 100 = 84 \% \hspace{20mm} (eq. 70).$$ The effect of ionic strength on total IC in soil solution through its effect on activity coefficients is greater than the effect of soil solution composition through its effect on $pK_H$. Even though the high concentration of ions in soil solution reduces solubility of $CO_2$, it increases the magnitude of dissociation relatively more. Neglecting the effect of composition of soil solution will cause underestimation of total IC rather than overestimation. On the other hand, if we decide to correct our calculations for ionic strength effect only because it is easier to calculate, our results will be overestimated by approx. 30%. Due to such complexity, it is recommended not to use gas chromatography when respiration rate is measured in highly saline soils. Instead, older and, unfortunately, more tedious method of soil incubation with cup containing strong alkali is recommended. # References Alva, A.K., Sumner, M.E., Miller, W.P., 1991.
